pg006_n0008: This textbook, Mathematics for Secondary Schools, is written specifically for Form One students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg006_n0009: The book is prepared in accordance with the 2023 Mathematics Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form I-IV, issued by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology.
pg006_n0010: It is a revised edition of Basic Mathematics for Secondary Schools Student’s Book for Form One that was published in 2019 in accordance with the 2005 syllabus issued by the then, Ministry of Education and Vocational Training (MoEVT).
pg006_n0012: The book consists of six (6) chapters, namely: Concept of Mathematics, Numbers, Approximations, Ratios and proportions, Algebra, and Coordinate geometry.
pg006_n0013: In addition to the contents, each chapter contains activities, illustrations, projects, and exercises.
pg006_n0014: You are encouraged to do all the activities, projects and attempt all questions in the exercises.
pg006_n0015: This will enhance your understanding and development of the intended competencies for this level.
pg006_n0017: Additional learning resources are available in the TIE library at https://ol.tie.go.tz or

pg007_im006: Introduction text box explaining that mathematics is all around us, used in many fields and technologies, and that the chapter covers the meaning, branches, relationships, and importance of mathematics in solving everyday problems.
pg007_n0012: Almost everything we do involves Mathematics.
pg007_n0013: It is applied in various fields such as science, engineering, technology, social studies, economics and many others.
pg007_n0014: Numerous devices such as mobile phones, computers, television sets, and satellites are designed and manufactured on the basis of mathematical knowledge.
pg007_n0015: In this chapter, you will learn about the meaning of Mathematics, branches of Mathematics, relationship between Mathematics and other subjects, and the importance of studying Mathematics.
pg007_n0016: The competencies developed will enable you to apply Mathematics knowledge and skills to solve daily life problems in different fields such as Agriculture, Entrepreneurship, Botany, Zoology, Music, History, Business, and many other fields.
pg007_n0020: The word ‘Mathematics’ comes from the Greek word ‘mathema’, meaning ‘which is learnt’ or ‘science, knowledge or learning’.
pg007_n0021: Numbers, measurements, shapes of physical objects, and equations form a small part of it.
pg007_n0022: Mathematics can be thought of as the science of the structures, orders, patterns, and relations that have evolved from elementary practices of counting, measuring, and describing the shapes of objects.
pg007_n0023: It can also be thought of as a language of science because by using mathematical reasoning, one can develop an understanding and be able to predict nature.
pg007_n0024: Mathematics has the ability to provide precise expression for every concept that can be formulated using mathematical symbols and structures.
pg007_n0025: The knowledge and skills of Mathematics play a crucial role in understanding the concepts of other subjects, both in sciences and arts.
pg007_n0029: Mathematics can be categorized into different branches such as Arithmetic, Algebra, and Geometry.
pg008_n0006: Arithmetic is a branch of Mathematics that deals with properties and manipulations of numbers.
pg008_n0007: Manipulation of numbers is achieved through the use of basic mathematical operations namely: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
pg008_n0011: Algebra is a branch of Mathematics in which arithmetic operations are applied to symbols rather than specific numbers.
pg008_n0012: The symbols or letters in algebra are called variables which represent quantities with no fixed values.
pg008_n0016: The word geometry was derived from the Greek word ‘Geo’, which means ‘earth’ and ‘metry’, which means ‘measurement’.
pg008_n0017: Therefore, Geometry is a branch of Mathematics which deals with the study of the sizes, shapes, positions, angles, and dimensions of different physical objects.
pg008_n0018: Moreover, properties of points, lines, planes, similarities, congruence, and shapes of different regular objects are also studied in Geometry.
pg008_n0020: Relationship between Mathematics and other subjects
pg008_n0022: Every aspect of our life makes use of Mathematics in one way or another.
pg008_n0023: Mathematics plays a major role as a tool for effective understanding of other subjects.
pg008_n0024: Numerous concepts in other subjects and fields are described precisely using Mathematics.
pg008_n0025: Learning Mathematics can also benefit students through developing their problem solving and critical thinking skills.
pg008_n0026: Note that, Mathematics formulas which are used to represent and describe concepts and scenarios in other fields are commonly referred to as mathematical models.
pg008_im003: Activity 1.1, “Discovering the use of Mathematics in daily lives,” with three tasks: recall daily activities and identify applications of mathematics; represent the activities and mathematical skills using a table or another method; and explain the mathematical aspects observed.
pg008_n0029: Activity 1.1: Discovering the use of Mathematics in daily lives
pg008_n0032: 1. Recall your daily activities, identify and record applications of Mathematics in such activities.
pg008_n0034: 2. Use a table or any method of your choice to represent the identified activities and its mathematical skills obtained in step 1.
pg008_n0036: 3. Explain the mathematical aspects you have observed in step 2.
pg008_n0040: Agriculture is closely related to Mathematics.
pg008_n0041: For instance, when farmers want to buy seeds, they need to understand the ratio of seeds that is sufficient per piece of land.
pg009_n0004: Similarly, the determination of the number of bags of fertilizers needed per acre requires some calculations.
pg009_n0005: In these two examples, Mathematics enables farmers to avoid the wastage of financial resources by purchasing only the required amount of inputs.
pg009_n0006: Mathematics is also used in Agriculture to determine suitable amount of water to be used in irrigation and the spacing between seedlings.
pg009_n0007: Similarly, Mathematics is used to determine the investment, expenditure, and savings in cultivating a specific crop, dividing a piece of land, calculating the cost of labour, and so forth.
pg009_n0011: There is a direct relationship between Mathematics and Biology.
pg009_n0012: For example, normal animal weights, rate of respiration, nutritive values of food, and transpiration are a few quantities in Biology that can be calculated using mathematical concepts.
pg009_n0013: Mathematics can also be used to estimate the number of blood cells present in the body, measurement of blood pressure, and counting sex chromosomes, among many others.
pg009_n0017: Mathematics is widely applied in Chemistry to represent and solve various problems.
pg009_n0018: Some Chemistry activities involve measurement of masses, volumes, lengths, temperatures and densities of matter.
pg009_n0019: Mathematics is also used to measure the constituents of mixtures, balancing chemical equations, among many other applications.
pg009_n0023: Physics involves the study of laws, principles, and theorems which governs how matter works.
pg009_n0024: Most of the quantities in Physics are expressed mathematically through formulas.
pg009_n0025: In order to understand how to apply the formulas to solve some physics challenges, knowledge of Mathematics is needed.
pg009_n0026: All the quantities in physics are expressed in numbers and units which have to be manipulated using the concepts and skills of Mathematics.
pg009_n0027: For example, to determine the speed of a moving object, one has to find a ratio between the distance covered and the time taken.
pg009_n0029: Mathematics and Information and Communications Technology
pg009_n0031: Mathematics plays a big role in the field of Information and Communications Technology (ICT).
pg009_n0032: Computer programs, applications, software, and computer languages make use of mathematical concepts.
pg009_n0033: A common example of the application of numbers is in defining colours in web development languages.
pg009_n0034: For instance, the HTML (hypertext markup language) and CSS (cascading style sheets) uses colour notations such as #000000 which represent Black, #008000 for Green and #800000 for Maroon.
pg009_n0035: Furthermore, the digits 0 and 1 are commonly used in computing systems in computers.
pg010_n0005: Mathematics is widely applied in daily life activities related to Business Studies.
pg010_n0006: For example, if one wants to determine profit or loss in business, a difference between the selling and buying prices is to be calculated.
pg010_n0007: If the buying price is less than the selling price, the business makes profit.
pg010_n0008: If the buying price is higher than the selling price, the business makes loss.
pg010_n0009: Mathematics is also applied in other areas such as in loan borrowing, determining prices of items, among many other applications.
pg010_n0012: Geographers require mathematical calculations to find the distance from one place to another, finding gradients, altitudes of hills and mountains.
pg010_n0013: Through mathematical calculations, geographical locations of different places are determined using latitudes and longitudes, and real-life objects such as buildings are represented on a map through the use of scales.
pg010_n0016: Mathematics helps in describing various historical activities such as duration of events and expressing historical events which happened at different points in time.
pg010_n0017: For example, a simple mathematical operation is used to determine duration of historical events such as World Wars, colonial periods and time spent by leaders in positions, determining dates and ages of fossils by using some mathematical principles such as carbon-14 among many other applications.
pg010_n0020: Mastering basic concepts of arithmetic can enable a person to understand better and manage literary works.
pg010_n0021: A kind of writing which can draw attention to readers depend on several factors such as number of words per sentence, the number of sentences per paragraph, and the number of paragraphs per page.
pg010_n0022: For example, 20 words in a sentence are considered as average.
pg010_n0023: Thus, in analysing writing style, one need to find an average number of words in each sentence, which requires Mathematics concepts.
pg010_n0026: The knowledge of Mathematics plays a vital role in music.
pg010_n0027: For instance, playing one note in piano has a different sound as when three harmonic notes are played together.
pg010_n0028: Music notes are distinguished mathematically by their different values.
pg011_n0003: A semibreve has four beats, a minim has two beats, crotchet has one beat, quaver has <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math> a bit, semi quaver has <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math> a bit, and so on.
pg011_n0004: Reading and playing music represented by notes in a music sheet depends on the mathematical ability to understand these values.
pg011_n0008: Mathematics is important in all forms of sports and games.
pg011_n0009: For example, in many sports and games, winners are those who have accumulated highest number of points.
pg011_n0010: Furthermore, in most of the sports and games, there are specific number of players in the playing ground.
pg011_n0011: For instance, a football team has 11 players while a netball team has 7 players.
pg011_n0012: Moreover, players in some games such as football are given names in terms of numbers.
pg011_n0013: In football, a goalkeeper is normally assigned number 1.
pg011_n0014: In addition, all playing grounds are prepared with specific standards of measurements.
pg011_n0016: Activity 1.2: Exploring the use of Mathematics in other fields
pg011_n0017: Explore various resources such as books and internet to discover examples of mathematical concepts and skills that are used in 3 subjects other than those discussed in this chapter.
pg011_n0021: Learning Mathematics and using mathematical skills in daily life enhances problem solving, critical thinking, effective time management among many other importances.
pg011_n0025: Financial management requires mathematical skills during the preparation of budgets.
pg011_n0026: Calculations are done to ensure the budget prepared correlates with the funds collected.
pg011_n0030: Problem-solving is one of the most important skills in life.
pg011_n0031: Mathematics is one of the most effective ways to increase analytical and logical thinking, which helps us to become better problem solvers.
pg011_n0035: Time management is a key to success for everyone.
pg011_n0036: Therefore, time must be carefully managed.
pg011_n0037: Mathematics helps to determine the time spent on every activity so as to maximize its efficiency.

pg013_n0009: Numbers play a vital role in everyday life.
pg013_n0010: Different activities are performed with the help of numbers.
pg013_n0011: Numbers are used to quantify and measure quantities.
pg013_n0012: For instance, length, mass, time, volume, and population are some of the quantities represented by numbers.
pg013_n0013: In this chapter, you will learn about rational, irrational, and real numbers.
pg013_n0014: You will also learn about repeating decimals, inequalities and absolute values of real numbers.
pg013_n0015: The competencies developed will enable you to perform daily life activities such as counting things, managing money, distributing items, and interpreting numbers based on contexts, and many other applications.
pg013_n0019: Numbers are classified into different categories.
pg013_n0020: Some categories of numbers that you have already learned include whole numbers, natural numbers, fractions, integers, and decimals.
pg013_n0021: Other major categories of numbers include rational, irrational, and real numbers.
pg013_n0022: Activity 2.1 enables you to identify categories of numbers from daily life activities.
pg013_n0029: Use different measuring tools such as tape measure, ruler, weighing balance, and measuring cylinders to measure lengths, masses, and volumes of different objects, respectively.
pg013_n0032: Record the measurements in task 1 and categorise them based on your understanding of categories of numbers.

pg014_n0007: Representation of rational numbers on a number line
pg014_n0009: Rational numbers can be represented on a number line.
pg014_n0010: Positive rational numbers are represented on the right of zero (the origin) and the negative rational numbers on the left of the origin.
pg014_n0011: The number line helps us to determine other rational numbers between any two rational numbers by increasing the number of divisions.

pg018_n0018: Study carefully the decimal part of the fractions and write down their unique characteristics.
pg018_n0020: A repeating decimal, also known as recurring decimal is a decimal number with at least one digit in the decimal part that repeats consecutively in a regular order without an end.
pg018_n0021: For instance, 1.6666666… and 0.639639639639… are repeating decimals because 6 and 639 digits from the two decimal numbers, respectively, in the decimal part repeat themselves without an end.
pg018_n0022: The three dots indicate that the repeating digits continue infinitely.
pg018_n0024: Repeating decimals can also be represented by using a dot or a bar that is placed on top of a repeating digit.
pg018_n0029: Write each of the following repeating decimals by using a dot and a bar.
pg018_n0045: 0.3333 is a repeating decimal which can be written as 0.3̇ or 0.<math><menclose notation="top" class="tml-overline"><mn>3</mn></menclose></math>
pg018_n0053: In Example 2.4, the digits with a dot or a bar are repeating infinitely.
pg018_n0054: In (b) and (c), it can be observed that if a group of digits is repeating, a dot should be put over the first and the last repeating digits.
pg018_n0056: Decimals are either terminating or non-terminating.
pg018_n0057: Terminating decimals have a definite number of digits after the decimal point while non-terminating decimals have an endless number of digits after the decimal point.
pg018_n0058: Thus, repeating decimals are non-terminating with one or more repeating digits in the decimal part.
pg019_n0004: Examples of terminating decimals are 0.5, 1.4, and 7.9 while non-terminating decimals are 3.1415926, 1.4142135, and 2.2360679…
pg019_n0008: When working with problems involving repeating decimals, it is important to convert them into simple fractions to maintain accuracy and avoid errors.
pg019_n0009: A repeating decimal can be converted into fraction using the following steps:
pg019_n0012: 1. Choose any variable to represent the required fraction.
pg019_n0014: 2. Multiply both sides of the equation by a multiple of 10 depending on the number of repeating decimals.

pg026_n0039: An irrational number is a number which can be written as a non-terminating and non-repeating decimal.
pg026_n0040: Also, these numbers cannot be expressed in the form of <math><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mfrac></math>, where <math><mi>a</mi></math> and <math><mi>b</mi></math> are integers and <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
pg026_n0041: The set of irrational numbers is denoted by <math><msup><mi>ℚ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em" class="tml-prime">′</mo></msup></math>.
pg026_n0042: Irrational numbers cannot be represented exactly on a number line.
pg026_n0043: However, they can always be approximated to rational numbers.

pg030_n0027: In Mathematics, an inequality is a statement that compares or relates two values or expressions.
pg030_n0028: The common terms involved in comparing the values or expressions are “less than”, “greater than”, “greater than or equal to”, “less than or equal to”, or “not equal to”.
pg030_n0029: For instance, the following statements are examples of inequalities:
pg030_n0034: (ii) John’s age is greater than Jane’s age.
pg030_n0036: (iii) x is less than or equal to 9.
pg030_n0038: (iv) y is greater than or equal to 0.
pg030_n0042: The mathematical statements can be written using symbols which represent inequalities as shown in the following table.
pg031_n0005: In general, mathematical statements which use ≠, >, <, ≥, or ≤ are called inequalities.
pg031_n0010: The sharp end of > and < always points to a smaller number.
pg031_n0012: The symbols ≤ and ≥ are sometimes referred to as at most and at least, respectively.
pg031_n0014: If the inequality is divided or multiplied both sides by a negative number, the direction of the inequality sign changes.

pg031_n0021: Generally, on a number line, a number to the right side of another number is always greater than a number to its left side.
pg031_n0022: Thus, from the number line, b is greater than a, which can also be written as <math><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>></mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>.
pg031_n0023: c is greater than b, which can also be written as <math><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>></mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
pg031_n0024: The vice versa is also true, that is, a number which is on the left side of another number on a number line is always less than the number on its right side.

pg034_n0065: Representing real numbers on a number line
pg034_n0067: Sometimes it is not easy to list all elements of a set of real numbers.
pg034_n0068: For example, it is not possible to list all real numbers which are greater than <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>.
pg034_n0069: However, the use of inequality symbols helps to define the elements in the given set.
pg034_n0070: In this case, if <math><mi>x</mi></math> is a real number which is greater than <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>, then <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> defines all the required elements in the set.
pg035_n0004: The inequality <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> means that there are infinitely many real numbers satisfying this condition.
pg035_n0005: Thus, they can be represented on a number line by using an arrow with a small circle at <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math> (initial point) since it is not included in the set.
pg035_n0007: The following number line shows all the real numbers which are greater than <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>.
pg035_n0019: A small circle (o) indicates that the number in a given set of real numbers is excluded in the given set.
pg035_n0020: This is always true for a set of real numbers which involve < or > inequality symbols.
pg035_n0022: A thick dot (●) indicates that the number in a given set of numbers is included in the given set.
pg035_n0023: This is always true for set of real numbers which involve ≤ or ≥ inequality symbols.

pg039_n0004: Absolute value of a real number
pg039_n0006: The absolute value of a real number <math><mi>x</mi></math>, denoted by <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>|</mi></mrow></math> is the non-negative value of <math><mi>x</mi></math> regardless of its sign.
pg039_im004: Number line from -2 to 2 with 0 at the center; arrows above show that the distance from 0 to -2 and from 0 to 2 is 2 units in each direction.
pg039_n0010: The distance from 0 to <math><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and that from 0 to 2 is the same, that is 2 units.
pg039_n0011: Thus, 2 is an absolute value of both 2 and <math><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
pg039_n0012: The absolute value of a number is the magnitude of that number regardless of its sign.
pg039_n0014: The absolute value of a number <math><mi>x</mi></math> is written as <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>|</mi></mrow></math> such that <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> if <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> if <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, and its distance is represented on a number line from 0.
pg039_n0015: This distance is always positive or zero.
pg039_n0017: For instance; <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mn>0.75</mn><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>0.143</mn><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.143</mn></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="true">|</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, and <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
pg039_n0019: In general, for any two positive and negative numbers <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, their absolute values are equal, that is, <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>|</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>|</mi></mrow></math>.
pg040_n0006: <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="true">|</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mfrac><mn>13</mn><mn>10</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="true">|</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mn>10</mn></mfrac><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg040_n0007: <math><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="true">|</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mfrac><mn>5</mn><mn>10</mn></mfrac><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg040_n0008: <math><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="true">|</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg040_n0011: Therefore, the absolute value of <math><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mfrac><mn>13</mn><mn>10</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></mrow></math> is <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>.

pg046_im005: Introduction box explaining that approximations are used in daily life for estimating costs, distances, ingredients, and other quantities, and that the chapter covers rounding by place value, decimal places, significant figures, and approximation in calculations.
pg046_n0010: Understanding approximations is important in our daily life.
pg046_n0011: Approximations are used in various real life situations like estimating cost of items, distances, and ingredients for a recipe.
pg046_n0012: In this chapter, you will learn about rounding off numbers by place values, number of decimal places and by significant figures.
pg046_n0013: Also, you will learn how to perform approximation in calculations.
pg046_n0014: The competencies developed will help you to perform real-life activities such as estimating number of things, analysing large data, making quick calculations, preparing budgets, and many other applications.
pg046_n0018: Approximation is a process of finding a number that is closest to the exact value.
pg046_n0019: It involves expressing a number into a higher or lower value which is close to the exact value.
pg046_n0020: Approximation can be termed as estimation and is represented by the symbol ‘≈’.

pg046_n0036: Rounding off numbers is a process of making a number simpler, but keeping its value closer to the original value.
pg046_n0037: The outcome is less precise but more user-friendly.
pg046_n0038: Rounding off the number can be done by considering place values, number of decimal places, and number of significant figures.
pg047_n0004: Rounding off numbers by place values
pg047_n0006: Rounding off numbers by place values is done by considering the given place value for both whole and decimal parts of a number.
pg047_n0007: Thus, for whole numbers, it can be done to the nearest ones, tens, hundreds, thousands or any other place value.
pg047_n0008: For decimal numbers, it can be done to the nearest tenths, hundredths, thousandths and so on.
pg047_n0009: The following are basic procedures for rounding off numbers by place values.
pg047_n0011: (a) If the digit to the right of the rounding digit is either 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4, then the digit at the required place value remains unchanged, and each digit to the right of it become zeros.
pg047_n0015: A rounding digit is the digit at a place where a number is supposed to be rounded off.

pg047_n0032: Thus, 591,622 to the nearest hundreds is 591,600.

pg051_n0035: Rounding off by number of decimal places
pg051_n0037: Rounding off decimals involves a similar process of rounding numbers by place values.
pg051_n0038: When rounding off decimals, the digits to the right of the given decimal place are dropped rather than being replaced by zeros.
pg051_n0040: In the process of rounding off, the following steps are used:
pg051_n0041: (a) If the digit after the rounding digit is either 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4, then the rounding digit remain unchanged, and all the other digits to the right are dropped.
pg051_n0050: The digit in the third decimal place is 6 and the nearest digit to the right is 4 which is less than 5.
pg051_n0051: In this case, 6 will remain unchanged and 4 is dropped.
pg052_n0003: (b) If the digit to the right of a rounding digit is greater than 5, then 1 is added to the rounding digit and other digits to the right are dropped.
pg052_n0010: The digit in the third decimal place is 3 and the nearest digit to the right is 8 which is greater than 5.
pg052_n0011: In this case, 1 is added to the rounding digit and each digit to the right is dropped.
pg052_n0014: (c) If the digit to the right of a rounding digit is 5, then the rounding digit is considered as follows:
pg052_n0017: (i) Add 1 to the rounding digit if it is odd.
pg052_n0019: (ii) Add 1 to the rounding digit (whether even or odd) if there are other digits that follow 5 which are all not zero.
pg052_n0021: (iii) The digit remains unchanged if all the digits following 5 are zeros and the rounding digit is even.

pg055_n0041: A significant figure is a digit in a number that gives information about the precision and accuracy of the measured value.
pg055_n0046: 1. Any digit from 1 to 9 appearing in a number is a significant figure.
pg055_n0048: 2. Each zero appearing in a number between digits 1 to 9 is a significant figure.
pg055_n0049: For example, 0 in 602 is a significant figure.
pg055_n0052: 3. When zeros are written to the right of the last non-zero digit, the zeros are not significant figures.
pg055_n0053: For example, 72,000 has only 2 significant figures.
pg055_n0055: 4. In decimals, any zero to the left of the first non-zero digit is not a significant figure.
pg055_n0056: For example, the zeros in 0.025 are not significant figures.
pg055_n0059: 5. All zeros that are on the right of a decimal point are significant only if a non-zero digit does not follow them.
pg055_n0060: For example, 0.040 has two significant figures while 0.6700 has four significant figures, and 10.000 has five significant figures.
pg056_n0007: When zero is written at the end of an approximated number, including decimals, it is a significant figure.
pg056_n0008: For example, 2.73 ≈ 3.0, and in this case, 0 is a significant figure.
pg056_n0009: Also, 45,961 ≈ 46,000, the zero at the third-place value is a significant figure.
pg056_n0013: All the zeros that are on the right of the non-zero digit are significant if they come from measurements.
pg056_n0014: For instance, 20 m has two significant figures and 300 g has 3 significant figures.
pg056_n0019: (i) Significant figures are also known as significant digits.
pg056_n0021: (ii) Significant figures are always counted from left towards the right of a number.
pg056_n0023: Rounding off numbers by significant figures
pg056_n0025: Rounding off numbers to a specified number of significant figures is one of the methods of approximations.
pg056_n0026: Similar rules for rounding off numbers are used in writing numbers to a given number of significant figures.

pg078_im005: Introduction to algebra: Algebra uses letters, numbers, and symbols to solve real-life problems involving unknown quantities. The chapter covers algebraic expressions, equations with one and two unknowns, and inequalities, with applications such as shopping, travel planning, recipes, profit and loss, and currency conversion.
pg078_n0009: Algebra is a branch of mathematics that helps to solve real-life problems by using letters, numbers, and symbols.
pg078_n0010: It unifies all branches of mathematics, and thus, it is a tool used in daily life activities.
pg078_n0011: Algebra is used to understand and work with unknown quantities in various situations.
pg078_n0012: For instance, it helps to calculate expenditure when shopping, plan travel routes, cooking or preparing recipes for different servings.
pg078_n0013: In this chapter, you will learn about algebraic expressions, equations with one unknown, equations with two unknowns, and inequalities with one unknown.
pg078_n0014: The competencies developed will enable you to solve daily life problems such as planning for recipes, scheduling routes, estimating profit and loss, currency conversions, among many other applications.
pg078_n0018: In algebra, letters or symbols are used to represent numbers.
pg078_n0019: For instance, it is common to represent the length of an object by the letter l, radius by letter r, and diameter by letter d.
pg078_n0020: In addition, letters such as x, y, z, α and β can be used to represent numbers.
pg078_n0022: An algebraic expression is a mathematical statement which contains numbers, letters and mathematical operations such as +, −, ×, and ÷.
pg078_n0023: An algebraic expression is made up of terms.
pg078_n0025: A term can be a number, a variable, a number multiplied by a variable, or a variable multiplied by a variable.
pg078_n0026: For example, in the algebraic expression 5x − 3y + 8, terms are 5x, −3y and 8.
pg078_n0027: Terms with the same variables and exponents are called like terms.
pg078_n0028: For example, 8y and 9y or 8xy and 3xy or 6x^2y and 2x^2y are like terms.
pg078_n0029: Terms with different variables or exponents are called unlike terms.
pg078_n0030: For example, 6x and 6z or 3 mn and 4vy or 6u^2y and 2uy^2 are unlike terms.
pg079_n0004: Simplification of algebraic expressions involves combining like terms by adding or subtracting their coefficients in order to obtain a simple term.
pg079_n0005: It may also involve multiplying and dividing terms as well as working with fractions and brackets.
pg079_n0007: Addition and subtraction of algebraic expressions
pg079_n0009: The basic principle of addition and subtraction of algebraic expressions is that, only like terms can be added or subtracted.

pg081_n0053: Just as 2 × 3 = 3 × 2, so is n × m = m × n and a × b = b × a = ab = ba.

pg086_n0019: An algebraic equation is a mathematical statement connecting two algebraic expressions with an equal sign (=).
pg086_n0020: It expresses a statement or a problem in a clear and short way.
pg086_n0021: For example, <math><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> are algebraic equations.
pg086_n0022: Therefore, an equation has two equal sides, the left-hand side and the right-hand side.
pg086_n0026: A linear equation is an algebraic equation in which each variable has an exponent of one.
pg086_n0027: A linear equation can have one or more unknown variables.
pg086_n0028: For example, <math><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>z</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> are linear equations with one variable <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>z</mi></math>, respectively, whereas <math><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> are linear equations with two variables <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>y</mi></math>.

pg096_n0046: Linear simultaneous equations are two or more algebraic equations which share the variables and the solutions.
pg096_n0047: They are called simultaneous equations because they are solved simultaneously and have common solution.
pg096_n0049: <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mspace width="2em"></mspace><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg096_n0051: Equation (1) involves two unknowns x and y.
pg096_n0052: Different values of x and y can be used to make the equation true.
pg096_n0053: The values of x and y that satisfy equation (1) in ordered pairs (x, y) are (1,19), (2,18), (3, 17), (10,10), (13.4, 6.6) and so on.
pg096_n0054: Therefore, in order to get unique values of x and y in equation (1), another linear equation is needed.
pg096_n0055: For instance, if it is also known that
pg096_n0056: <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mspace width="2em"></mspace><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg096_n0058: It is possible to use equation (1) and (2) to find the unique values of x and y which satisfy both equations.
pg096_n0059: These equations are such that the value of x in equation (1) is the same as the value of x in equation (2) and the same applies to y, that is, the equations have common solution.
pg097_n0007: There are several methods of solving simultaneous equations.
pg097_n0008: This section discusses how solutions of linear simultaneous equations are obtained by elimination and substitution methods.
pg097_n0010: Solving linear simultaneous equations by elimination method
pg097_n0012: Elimination method involves performing suitable mathematical operations to reduce the two equations into a single equation with one unknown.
pg097_n0013: The following are the steps for solving linear simultaneous equations by elimination method:
pg097_n0017: Choose the easiest variable to be eliminated.
pg097_n0018: Multiply the given equations by suitable numbers so as to make the coefficients of the chosen variable in both equations equal.
pg097_im004: Steps 2 to 4 of the elimination method: add the new equations if the coefficients of the variable to be eliminated have opposite signs, otherwise subtract them; solve the resulting equation to find one unknown; then repeat the process to find the second unknown. Note: some simultaneous equations can be converted into linear equations by changing the variables.
pg097_n0021: Add the new equations if the coefficients of the chosen variable to be eliminated are opposite in signs, otherwise subtract them.
pg097_n0024: This gives the value of one of the unknowns.
pg097_n0026: Repeat steps 1 to 3 for the value of the second unknown.
pg097_n0028: Some simultaneous equations can be converted into linear equations by changing the variables.
pg097_im005: Example 5.30: Solve the simultaneous equations 6x plus y equals 15 and 3x plus y equals 9 by elimination. The solution begins by labeling the equations as (1) and (2), choosing x to eliminate, and noting that the coefficients of x are 6 and 3.

pg102_n0007: Solving linear simultaneous equations by substitution method
pg102_n0009: Substitution method involves choosing one equation and transposing one of its variables by making it the subject of the other.
pg102_n0010: The resulting equation is substituted into the other to obtain a single equation with one unknown.
pg102_n0011: The following are the steps for solving simultaneous equations of two unknowns by substitution method.
pg102_n0015: Express one of the variables in terms of the other from one of the equations.
pg102_n0018: Substitute the equation obtained in Step 1 into the second equation to obtain an equation in one unknown.
pg102_n0021: Solve the equation in one unknown obtained in Step 2.
pg102_n0024: Substitute the value of the variable obtained in Step 3 to one of the equations to get the value of the other unknown.

pg104_n0028: Solving word problems on linear simultaneous equations
pg104_n0030: Simultaneous equations are useful in solving real-life problems involving more than one unknown which can be solved simultaneously.
pg104_n0031: Such problems can be formulated from different real-life scenarios such as the routes of the journey, managing multiple loans, recipe proportions and many others.
pg104_n0032: Formulating and solving word problems on simultaneous equations involve the following steps:
pg104_n0035: 1. Let the unknowns be represented by variables.
pg104_n0037: 2. Write the two simultaneous equations according to the requirements of the problem.
pg105_n0003: 4. Give the conclusion according to the demand of the problem.
pg105_n0008: The age of a father is four times the age of his son.
pg105_n0009: If the sum of their ages is 60 years, find the age of the son and that of the father.
pg105_n0013: Let <math><mi>x</mi></math> be the age of the son and <math><mi>y</mi></math> be the age of the father.
pg105_n0015: <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mspace width="2em"></mspace><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg105_n0016: <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn><mspace width="2em"></mspace><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
pg105_n0031: Therefore, the son’s age is 12 years and the father’s age is 48 years.
pg105_n0036: The sum of two numbers is 30.

pg106_n0011: Dashi has 83,000 Tanzanian shillings for shopping.

pg106_n0014: Find the price of a tie and a shirt.
pg106_n0018: Let: <math><mi>p</mi></math> be the price of a tie in Tanzanian shillings.
pg106_n0019: <math><mi>r</mi></math> be the price of a shirt in Tanzanian shillings.
pg106_n0021: It implies that for the first option, the cost for 2 ties is Tshs <math><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and the cost for 2 shirts is Tshs <math><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>.
pg106_n0023: Thus, the total cost for 2 ties and 2 shirts is <math><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>.
pg106_n0024: For the second option, the cost for 1 tie is Tshs <math><mi>p</mi></math> and the cost for 3 shirts is Tshs <math><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>.
pg106_n0026: Therefore, the total cost for 1 tie and 3 shirts is <math><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>.

pg114_n0069: Algebra uses letters or symbols to represent numbers in mathematical statements called algebraic expressions and equations.

pg115_n0006: 3. A term of an algebraic expression can be a single letter, or letters multiplied by numbers, or a constant separated by addition or subtraction.

pg115_n0010: 5. Simplification of an algebraic expression is a process of combining like terms to obtain a single term as possible.

pg121_n0009: Coordinate geometry is the branch of Mathematics which helps to uniquely determine the positions and movements of objects.
pg121_n0010: It also helps to understand the relationship between points on a plane using ordered pairs of coordinates.
pg121_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn about gradient or slope of a straight line, equation of a straight line, graphing straight lines as well as solving linear simultaneous equations graphically.
pg121_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you in solving problems such as plotting and analysing graphs, surveying and locating places, locating plot boundaries, interpreting traffic information, constructing buildings and roads and many other applications.
pg121_n0016: Coordinate geometry uses ordered pairs of numbers to describe the positions of points on the xy-coordinate plane.
pg121_n0017: The xy-coordinate plane or xy-plane is made up of two lines intersecting at right angles as shown in Figure 6.1.
pg121_im003: Chapter Six page titled 'Coordinate geometry,' with an introduction and a graph of the xy-coordinate plane showing the x- and y-axes intersecting at the origin and dividing the plane into four quadrants labeled I, II, III, and IV.
pg122_n0004: Each point on a plane is uniquely represented by means of an ordered pair of real numbers called the coordinates of a point.
pg122_n0005: The xy-plane is divided into four parts called quadrants as shown in Figure 6.1.
pg122_n0006: The first quadrant (I) has positive values of x and y, the second quadrant (II) has negative values of x and positive values of y.
pg122_n0007: The third quadrant (III) has all negative values of x and y and the fourth quadrant (IV) has x positive values and y negative values.
pg122_n0008: Recall that, the positions of points on the xy-plane are determined by using the x and y coordinates.
pg122_n0009: For example, for the point (4, 6), the first number 4 represents a distance from the origin along the x-axis and 6 represents a distance from the origin along the y-axis.

pg126_n0011: A straight line is formed by joining two distinct points.
pg126_n0012: Any two points lying on the straight line can be used to define it.
pg126_n0013: The nature of the straight line is described by its gradient.
pg126_n0014: That is, it can be horizontal, vertical or slanted.
pg126_n0015: The concept of gradient is applicable in many real-life activities such as lifting heavy loads, climbing mountains, determining steepness during road construction and many other applications.
pg126_n0016: Engage in Activity 6.2 to learn how to recognise the gradient of a straight line.

pg126_n0032: The other name of gradient is slope.

pg138_n0028: Let <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
pg138_n0029: It follows that <math><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, and <math><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>.
pg138_n0030: <math><mrow><mtext>Thus, </mtext><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
pg139_n0012: Therefore, the equation of the straight line is <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>.
pg139_n0017: Find the equation of a straight line which passes through the points A (3, 7) and B (–2, –3).
pg139_n0021: Using the formula for finding an equation of a straight line,
pg139_n0024: Let <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3,7</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
pg139_n0025: Substitute these values into the equation as follows:
pg139_n0026: <math><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
pg139_n0029: <math><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
pg139_n0032: Cross multiply and rearrange to get, <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
pg139_n0034: Therefore, the equation of the line passing through the given points is <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
pg140_n0009: A straight line passes through the points P(−4,5) and Q(−2,1).
pg140_n0021: (a) The gradient of the line is given by:
pg140_n0024: Let <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>4,5</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>2,1</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
pg140_n0026: <math><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
pg140_n0030: Therefore, the gradient of a straight line is −2.
pg140_n0032: (b) Let <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> be any point on the line.
pg140_n0033: Take the points P(−4, 5) and <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> to determine the equation of the line, that is,
pg140_n0034: <math><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
pg140_n0047: Therefore, the equation of the straight line is <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
pg141_n0005: (c) From the equation <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-intercept is obtained by setting <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> in the equation.
pg141_n0009: Therefore, the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-intercept is <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
pg141_n0014: Therefore, the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-intercept is <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="true">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></math>.
pg141_n0019: Verify that <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> represents an equation of the straight line passing through the point <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3,7</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, hence determine its gradient and <math><mi>y</mi></math>-intercept.

pg143_n0032: Equation in the form <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is sometimes referred to as slope-intercept equation.
pg143_n0033: Equation of straight line can also be expressed in a general form.
pg143_n0034: Referring equations (1) and (2) which have same gradient, that is:
pg143_n0035: <math display="block" class="tml-display" style="display:block math;"><mtable displaystyle="true" style="width:100%;"><mtr class="tml-tageqn"><mtd style="padding:0;width:50%;"></mtd><mtd><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mtd><mtd style="padding:0;width:50%;"><mtext class="tml-tag">(4)</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></math>
pg143_n0037: Equation (4) can be rearranged to get,
pg143_n0038: <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
pg143_n0040: Since <math><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, <math><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, <math><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, and <math><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are given real numbers, then <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, <math><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, and <math><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> are also real numbers.
pg143_n0041: Thus, they can be replaced by constants <math><mi>a</mi></math>, <math><mi>b</mi></math>, and <math><mi>c</mi></math>, respectively.
pg143_n0042: Therefore, the equation can be reduced to
pg143_n0043: <math display="block" class="tml-display" style="display:block math;"><mtable displaystyle="true" style="width:100%;"><mtr class="tml-tageqn"><mtd style="padding:0;width:50%;"></mtd><mtd><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd style="padding:0;width:50%;"><mtext class="tml-tag">(5)</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></math>
pg143_n0045: Equation (5) is called the general equation of a straight line.

pg144_n0012: Let <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
pg144_n0024: Therefore, the equation of the line is <math><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>21</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
pg144_n0029: Find the equation of a line passing through the points <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>,
pg144_n0030: giving your answer in the form <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>.
pg144_n0033: Let <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

pg164_n0022: The average of two numbers <math><mi>x</mi></math> and <math><mi>y</mi></math> is 7 and three times <math><mi>y</mi></math> subtracted from <math><mi>x</mi></math> is 18.
pg164_n0028: It follows that, the average of two numbers is <math><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> and three times when <math><mi>y</mi></math> is substracted from <math><mi>x</mi></math> is <math><mrow><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow></math>.
pg165_n0005: Thus, the two equations are <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>.

pg167_n0009: The xy-coordinate plane or xy-plane is made up of two number lines intersecting at right angles.
pg167_n0012: The horizontal axis is called the x-axis.
pg167_n0015: The vertical axis is called the y-axis.
pg167_n0018: The point at which the two axes intersect is called the origin.
pg167_n0021: The two axes divide the xy-plane into four equal parts called quadrants.
pg167_n0024: Each coordinate point in the coordinate plane has two numbers called coordinates written as an ordered pair <math><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
pg167_n0027: The formula for calculating the gradient or slope is
pg167_n0031: A vertical line has an undefined gradient and is parallel to the y-axis.
pg167_n0034: A horizontal line has a gradient whose value is 0 and is parallel to the x-axis.
pg167_n0037: The equation of a line can be written in the form <math><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, where <math><mi>m</mi></math> is the gradient and <math><mi>c</mi></math> is a constant.
pg167_n0040: The general equation of a line has the form <math><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.

pg006_n0008_easy_read: This textbook, Mathematics for Secondary Schools, is written for Form One students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg006_n0009_easy_read: The book follows the 2023 Mathematics Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form I-IV, from the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology.
pg006_n0010_easy_read: This book is a revised edition of Basic Mathematics for Secondary Schools Student’s Book for Form One. That book was published in 2019. It followed the 2005 syllabus from the then Ministry of Education and Vocational Training (MoEVT).
pg006_n0012_easy_read:
The book has 6 chapters:
- Concept of Mathematics
- Numbers
- Approximations
- Ratios and proportions
- Algebra
- Coordinate geometry
pg006_n0013_easy_read:
Each chapter also has:
- activities
- illustrations
- projects
- exercises
pg006_n0014_easy_read: You are encouraged to do all the activities and projects. You are also encouraged to try all the questions in the exercises.
pg006_n0015_easy_read: This will help you understand more. It will also help you develop the intended competencies for this level.
pg006_n0017_easy_read: You can find additional learning resources in the TIE library at https://ol.tie.go.tz or
pg007_n0012_easy_read: Mathematics is part of almost everything we do.
pg007_n0013_easy_read:
People use Mathematics in many fields, such as:
- science
- engineering
- technology
- social studies
- economics
- many others
pg007_n0014_easy_read:
Many devices use mathematical knowledge in their design and making, such as:
- mobile phones
- computers
- television sets
- satellites
pg007_n0015_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn about:
- the meaning of Mathematics
- the branches of Mathematics
- the relationship between Mathematics and other subjects
- the importance of studying Mathematics
pg007_n0016_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you use Mathematics to solve daily life problems in different fields, such as:
- Agriculture
- Entrepreneurship
- Botany
- Zoology
- Music
- History
- Business
- many other fields
pg007_n0020_easy_read:
The word ‘Mathematics’ comes from the Greek word ‘mathema’.
It means ‘which is learnt’ or ‘science, knowledge or learning’.
pg007_n0021_easy_read: Numbers, measurements, shapes of physical objects, and equations are only a small part of Mathematics.
pg007_n0022_easy_read:
Mathematics can be seen as the science of:
- structures
- order
- patterns
- relations
These ideas grew from simple activities like counting, measuring, and describing the shapes of objects.
pg007_n0023_easy_read:
Mathematics can also be seen as a language of science.
By using mathematical reasoning, people can understand things better and predict nature.
pg007_n0024_easy_read: Mathematics can give a precise expression for every concept that people can write with mathematical symbols and structures.
pg007_n0025_easy_read: Mathematics knowledge and skills are very important for understanding ideas in other subjects, in both sciences and arts.
pg007_n0029_easy_read:
Mathematics has different branches, such as:
- Arithmetic
- Algebra
- Geometry
pg008_n0006_easy_read: Arithmetic is a branch of Mathematics. It deals with the properties of numbers and how people use numbers.
pg008_n0007_easy_read:
People work with numbers by using basic math operations:
- addition
- subtraction
- multiplication
- division
pg008_n0011_easy_read: Algebra is a branch of Mathematics. In algebra, people use symbols instead of specific numbers in arithmetic operations.
pg008_n0012_easy_read: The symbols or letters in algebra are called variables. Variables stand for quantities that do not have fixed values.
pg008_n0016_easy_read:
The word geometry comes from 2 Greek words:
- ‘Geo’, which means ‘earth’
- ‘metry’, which means ‘measurement’
pg008_n0017_easy_read: So, Geometry is a branch of Mathematics. It studies the sizes, shapes, positions, angles, and dimensions of physical objects.
pg008_n0018_easy_read:
Geometry also studies:
- points
- lines
- planes
- similarities
- congruence
- shapes of different regular objects
pg008_n0022_easy_read: Mathematics is used in every part of our lives.
pg008_n0023_easy_read: Mathematics is very important for understanding other subjects well.
pg008_n0024_easy_read: Mathematics is used to describe many concepts in other subjects and fields in a precise way.
pg008_n0025_easy_read: Learning Mathematics can help students develop problem-solving skills and critical thinking skills.
pg008_n0026_easy_read: Mathematics formulas can represent and describe concepts and situations in other fields. These formulas are commonly called mathematical models.
pg008_n0032_easy_read: 1. Think about your daily activities. Identify and write down how Mathematics is used in those activities.
pg008_n0034_easy_read: 2. Use a table or another method you choose. Show the activities you identified and the mathematical skills from step 1.
pg008_n0036_easy_read: 3. Explain the mathematical parts you observed in step 2.
pg008_n0040_easy_read: Agriculture is closely connected to Mathematics.
pg008_n0041_easy_read: For example, when farmers want to buy seeds, they need to understand the ratio of seeds that is enough for each piece of land.
pg009_n0004_easy_read: To find the number of bags of fertilizer needed for 1 acre, you need to do some calculations.
pg009_n0005_easy_read: In these 2 examples, Mathematics helps farmers avoid wasting money. Farmers buy only the amount of inputs they need.
pg009_n0006_easy_read:
Mathematics is also used in Agriculture to find:
- the right amount of water for irrigation
- the space between seedlings
pg009_n0007_easy_read:
Mathematics is also used for these tasks:
- finding the investment, expenditure, and savings for growing a specific crop
- dividing a piece of land
- calculating the cost of labor
pg009_n0011_easy_read: Mathematics and Biology are directly related.
pg009_n0012_easy_read:
For example, Mathematics can be used in Biology to calculate:
- normal animal weights
- rate of respiration
- nutritive values of food
- transpiration
pg009_n0013_easy_read:
Mathematics can also be used to:
- estimate the number of blood cells in the body
- measure blood pressure
- count sex chromosomes
pg009_n0017_easy_read: Mathematics is widely used in Chemistry to show and solve different problems.
pg009_n0018_easy_read:
Some Chemistry activities involve measuring:
- mass
- volume
- length
- temperature
- density of matter
pg009_n0019_easy_read:
Mathematics is also used to:
- measure the parts of mixtures
- balance chemical equations
- do many other tasks
pg009_n0023_easy_read: Physics is the study of laws, principles, and theorems that explain how matter works.
pg009_n0024_easy_read: Most quantities in Physics are shown with formulas.
pg009_n0025_easy_read: To understand how to use formulas to solve some Physics problems, you need knowledge of Mathematics.
pg009_n0026_easy_read: All quantities in Physics are written with numbers and units. You use Mathematics concepts and skills to work with them.
pg009_n0027_easy_read: For example, to find the speed of a moving object, you find the ratio between the distance covered and the time taken.
pg009_n0031_easy_read: Mathematics plays a big role in Information and Communications Technology (ICT).
pg009_n0032_easy_read: Computer programs, applications, software, and computer languages use mathematical concepts.
pg009_n0033_easy_read: A common use of numbers is to define colors in web development languages.
pg009_n0034_easy_read:
For example, HTML (hypertext markup language) and CSS (cascading style sheets) use color notations such as:
- #000000 for Black
- #008000 for Green
- #800000 for Maroon
pg009_n0035_easy_read: Also, the digits 0 and 1 are commonly used in computer computing systems.
pg010_n0005_easy_read: Mathematics is used a lot in daily life activities related to Business Studies.
pg010_n0006_easy_read: For example, to find profit or loss in business, calculate the difference between the selling price and the buying price.
pg010_n0007_easy_read: If the buying price is lower than the selling price, the business makes a profit.
pg010_n0008_easy_read: If the buying price is higher than the selling price, the business makes a loss.
pg010_n0009_easy_read:
Mathematics is also used in other areas, such as:
- borrowing loans
- finding the prices of items
- many other uses
pg010_n0012_easy_read:
Geographers use mathematical calculations to find:
- the distance from 1 place to another
- gradients
- the heights of hills and mountains
pg010_n0013_easy_read: Mathematical calculations help people find the locations of different places by using latitude and longitude. Mathematical calculations also help show real objects, such as buildings, on a map by using scales.
pg010_n0016_easy_read: Mathematics helps describe historical activities, such as how long events lasted and when historical events happened.
pg010_n0017_easy_read:
For example, a simple mathematical operation is used to find:
- how long historical events lasted, such as World Wars and colonial periods
- how long leaders stayed in positions
- the dates and ages of fossils by using mathematical principles such as carbon-14
- many other things
pg010_n0020_easy_read: Learning basic arithmetic can help a person understand and manage literary works better.
pg010_n0021_easy_read:
A type of writing that can attract readers depends on several factors, such as:
- the number of words in each sentence
- the number of sentences in each paragraph
- the number of paragraphs on each page
pg010_n0022_easy_read: For example, 20 words in a sentence is considered average.
pg010_n0023_easy_read: So, when a person analyzes writing style, the person needs to find the average number of words in each sentence. This uses mathematics concepts.
pg010_n0026_easy_read: Knowledge of Mathematics is very important in music.
pg010_n0027_easy_read: For example, 1 note played on a piano sounds different from 3 harmonic notes played together.
pg010_n0028_easy_read: Music notes are told apart mathematically by their different values.
pg011_n0003_easy_read:
A semibreve has 4 beats.
A minim has 2 beats.
A crotchet has 1 beat.
A quaver has <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math> beat.
A semi quaver has <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math> beat.
And so on.
pg011_n0004_easy_read: To read and play music from notes on a music sheet, you need to understand these values in Mathematics.
pg011_n0008_easy_read: Mathematics is important in all sports and games.
pg011_n0009_easy_read: For example, in many sports and games, the winners are the players or teams with the highest number of points.
pg011_n0010_easy_read: Also, most sports and games have a specific number of players on the playing ground.
pg011_n0011_easy_read:
For example, a football team has 11 players.
A netball team has 7 players.
pg011_n0012_easy_read: Also, in some games such as football, players are identified by numbers.
pg011_n0013_easy_read: In football, the goalkeeper is usually given number 1.
pg011_n0014_easy_read: Also, all playing grounds are made using specific measurement standards.

pg018_n0020_easy_read: A repeating decimal, also called a recurring decimal, is a decimal number with at least 1 digit in the decimal part that repeats in the same order without ending.
pg018_n0021_easy_read:
For example, 1.6666666… and 0.639639639639… are repeating decimals.
They are repeating decimals because, in the decimal part, 6 repeats without end in the first number, and 639 repeats without end in the second number.
pg018_n0022_easy_read: The 3 dots show that the repeating digits go on forever.
pg018_n0024_easy_read: You can also show repeating decimals by putting a dot or a bar over the repeating digit.

pg018_n0056_easy_read: Decimals are either terminating or non-terminating.
pg018_n0057_easy_read:
Terminating decimals have a fixed number of digits after the decimal point.
Non-terminating decimals have digits after the decimal point that do not end.
pg018_n0058_easy_read: So, repeating decimals are non-terminating decimals with 1 or more digits that repeat in the decimal part.
pg019_n0004_easy_read:
Examples of terminating decimals are:
- 0.5
- 1.4
- 7.9
Examples of non-terminating decimals are:
- 3.1415926
- 1.4142135
- 2.2360679…

- "greater than"
- "greater than or equal to"
- "less than or equal to"
- "not equal to"

pg031_n0005_easy_read: In general, mathematical statements that use ≠, >, <, ≥, or ≤ are called inequalities.
pg031_n0010_easy_read: The pointed end of > and < always points to the smaller number.
pg031_n0012_easy_read: The symbols ≤ and ≥ are sometimes called at most and at least.
pg031_n0014_easy_read: If you divide or multiply both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the inequality sign changes direction.

pg039_n0010_easy_read: The distance from 0 to <math><mrow><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> is the same as the distance from 0 to 2. The distance is 2 units.

pg039_n0012_easy_read: The absolute value of a number is the size of the number without its sign.
pg039_n0014_easy_read:
The absolute value of a number <math><mi>x</mi></math> is written as <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>|</mi></mrow></math>.
If <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
If <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
On a number line, <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>|</mi></mrow></math> shows the distance from 0.
pg039_n0015_easy_read: This distance is always positive or 0.
pg039_n0017_easy_read:
For example:
- <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mn>0.75</mn><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow></math>
- <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>0.143</mn><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.143</mn></mrow></math>
- <math><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="true">|</mo><mo form="prefix" stretchy="false">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>
- <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
- <math><mrow><mi>|</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>|</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>

pg046_n0010_easy_read: Understanding approximations is important in daily life.
pg046_n0011_easy_read:
People use approximations in real life.
For example:
- estimating the cost of items
- estimating distances
- estimating ingredients for a recipe
pg046_n0012_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn about rounding numbers by:
- place value
- number of decimal places
- significant figures
pg046_n0013_easy_read: You will also learn how to use approximation in calculations.
pg046_n0014_easy_read:
These skills will help you in real-life activities.
For example:
- estimating the number of things
- analyzing large data
- making quick calculations
- preparing budgets
- many other uses
pg046_n0018_easy_read: Approximation is the process of finding the number that is closest to the exact value.
pg046_n0019_easy_read: In approximation, you change a number to a higher or lower value that is close to the exact value.
pg046_n0020_easy_read:
Approximation can also be called estimation.
Its symbol is ‘≈’.

pg046_n0036_easy_read: Rounding off numbers is the process of making a number simpler, while keeping it close to the original value.
pg046_n0037_easy_read: The result is less exact but easier to use.
pg046_n0038_easy_read:
You can round off a number by looking at:
- place value
- number of decimal places
- number of significant figures
pg047_n0006_easy_read: To round a number by place value, look at the place value you are asked to use. Do this for whole numbers and decimal numbers.
pg047_n0007_easy_read:
For whole numbers, you can round to these place values:
- ones
- tens
- hundreds
- thousands
- any other place value
pg047_n0008_easy_read:
For decimal numbers, you can round to these place values:
- tenths
- hundredths
- thousandths
- and more

pg051_n0037_easy_read: Rounding decimals uses a similar process to rounding numbers by place value.
pg051_n0038_easy_read:
When you round decimals, drop the digits to the right of the decimal place you are rounding to.
Do not replace them with zeros.
pg051_n0040_easy_read: Use these steps to round off:
pg051_n0041_easy_read:
(a) If the digit after the rounding digit is 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4, the rounding digit stays the same.
Drop all the digits to the right.
pg051_n0050_easy_read:
The digit in the 3rd decimal place is 6.
The digit to the right is 4, and 4 is less than 5.
pg051_n0051_easy_read: In this case, 6 stays the same and 4 is dropped.
pg052_n0003_easy_read: (b) If the digit to the right of the rounding digit is more than 5, add 1 to the rounding digit. Then remove the digits to the right.
pg052_n0010_easy_read: The digit in the third decimal place is 3. The digit to its right is 8. The digit 8 is more than 5.
pg052_n0011_easy_read: In this case, add 1 to the rounding digit. Then remove each digit to the right.
pg052_n0014_easy_read: (c) If the digit to the right of the rounding digit is 5, use these rules:
pg052_n0017_easy_read: (i) Add 1 to the rounding digit if the rounding digit is odd.
pg052_n0019_easy_read: (ii) Add 1 to the rounding digit, whether it is even or odd, if there are other digits after 5 and they are not all 0.
pg052_n0021_easy_read: (iii) Keep the rounding digit the same if all the digits after 5 are 0 and the rounding digit is even.
